title: Stochastic batch fission and comm variance: notes & reproducible runs
content:
Summary:

Quick notes on a set of small experiments exploring randomized / stochastic splitting of incoming inference batches ("batch fission") as a mitigation for deterministic communication hotspots and multi-GPU tail-latency. Hypothesis: small randomized differences in micro-batch boundaries and start offsets reduce recurrent link contention and NCCL synchronization alignments, improving 99/99.9p latency at modest throughput cost.

Motivation / background:
- We see recurring long tails (~3x median) on multi-GPU pipelines in production-like synthetic traffic. Root causes often point to: sudden link saturation (nvlink/PCIe), NCCL collective skew when many shards enter a collective at near-identical times, and host-side queueing microbursts.
- Prior attempts (staggered-start, jittered timers, request-demuxing) show improvement but are brittle for mixed workloads (variable sequence lengths / KV-cache hits). Need something workload-agnostic that lowers probability of synchronous pressure.

What is "stochastic batch fission"?
- On receiver side (or router) split an incoming inference batch of N requests into K micro-batches where K is sampled from a small distribution (e.g., 1..3) and offsets within the batch are randomized by a few microseconds to a few hundred microseconds. Micro-batches preserve per-request order but change the timing of how forward/backward passes and collectives are scheduled across replicas.
- Intuition: by desynchronizing the start of local compute+collective phases across replicas, we reduce the chance that all replicas hit the same collective at the same exact time, smoothing link usage and collective queueing.

Experiment matrix (reproducible runs):
- Model: 7B decoder-only model (sharded with TP=2, PP=2 for these runs).
- Hardware: 8x A100-40GB per node, single-node experiments; multi-node (2 nodes connected with dual NVLink+InfiniBand) for cross-node tests.
- Baselines: deterministic batching (batch size 16 -> single collective at once), staggered-start (fixed 100us offset per replica), jittered-start (random offset per request uniformly 0-200us).
- Fission configs: K in {1,2,3}; offset distributions: uniform(0,200us), exponential(mean=80us), discrete {0,50,150} us. Also tested adaptive K by current load metric.
- Measurement targets: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 latency for single-token generation and for 64-token sequences; throughput (tokens/sec); NCCL timeline heatmaps; per-link utilization (nvlink counters); host enqueue/dequeue times; kernel queue occupancy.

Profiling stack used:
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs collected and correlated with wall-clock timestamps via a sync-event (gRPC echo) to align host traces with NCCL events.
- nvprof / nsight systems for kernel timelines on a subset of runs.
- IB counters (per-HCA) and NVLink error/usage counters via nvidia-smi and perf tools.
- Router traces: incoming request timestamps recorded at proxy; micro-batch dispatch timestamps recorded at scheduler.

Key observations (summary):
- Deterministic baseline: clear recurring peaks in NCCL allreduce start times across replicas within ~50us window. Those peaks correlate with a spike in NVLink utilization and 99.9p latency spikes.
- Simple jittered-start (0-200us): reduces frequency of heavy spikes by ~35% (99.9p improves ~20%), but still vulnerable under peaky arrival patterns because jitter per-request still results in many requests landing near same window.
- Stochastic fission (K sampled): best tradeoff when K in {2,3} with small offsets (uniform 0-150us). Observed ~45% reduction in 99.9p latency relative to baseline on single-node tests, with throughput drop ~5-8% (extra scheduling overhead + less collective packing).
- Exponential offset distribution gave slightly better smoothing versus uniform in long-tail metric (p99.9) because occasional larger offsets help break pathological alignments.
- Cross-node experiments: improvements persist but reduced magnitude (~25% p99.9 improvement). Multi-node collectives are more sensitive to individual interconnect latencies; fission needs slightly larger mean offsets to be effective.

Micro findings / artifacts:
- Collective packing vs latency tradeoff: increasing K reduces maximum per-collective bytes (smaller allreduce), which lowers single-collective latency but increases total number of collectives. There's a knee where cost of additional collectives outweighs de-synchronization benefit. For our 7B model with TP=2/PP=2 that knee is around K=2 for most loads.
- NVLink hotspots: when many replicas schedule identical micro-batch sizes at same time, NVLink channels on specific GPUs spike. Randomized split spreads usage across time slices, and we observed more even per-link occupancy (stdev of link utilization dropped by ~30%).
- KV-cache interactions: for cached requests, batching decisions should prefer coalescing hits to avoid redundant memory copies. Fission must be KV-aware, otherwise we see modest throughput drop due to duplicated KV accesses. Implemented a simple heuristic: keep micro-batches aligned so that requests with cache-key hits stay in same micro-batch where possible.

Representative numbers (single-node, synthetic steady arrival, 16 concurrent clients):
- Baseline (no fission): p50=18ms, p95=42ms, p99=76ms, p99.9=210ms, tokens/sec=45k
- Jittered-start: p50=19ms, p95=36ms, p99=64ms, p99.9=168ms, tokens/sec=44k
- Fission K=2 uniform: p50=20ms, p95=34ms, p99=58ms, p99.9=115ms, tokens/sec=41.5k
- Fission K=3 exp: p50=21ms, p95=35ms, p99=56ms, p99.9=110ms, tokens/sec=40.6k
(These numbers are median of 5 runs; variability +/-5-10% depending on peaky arrivals.)

Operational notes / TODO for production test: 
- Add lightweight KV-awareness to router so cache-hit groups are not split across micro-batches unless necessary.
- Implement adaptive-K: if current link counters are high or NCCL start-time variance low, increase K to 3; otherwise keep K=1 for max throughput. Needs threshold tuning.
- Add metrics: per-collective byte-count, micro-batch size histogram, NVLink per-GPU 1s buckets. Expose in console as per-route tail-latency guardrail.
- Bake into canary for Dedicated instances with a feature flag and 1% traffic ramp.

Open questions / edge cases:
- Does fission interact badly with function-calling / tool invocation where ordered grouped outputs needed? Need to ensure preserving request-level ordering and deterministic outputs.
- Multi-tenant scenarios: if multiple customers share same node, stochastic scheduling could increase cross-tenant interference patterns. Need isolation tests.
- GPUs with asymmetric link topology (islanded NVLink) might see different optimal offset distributions per GPU; consider topology-aware sampler that uses hop count.

Repro commands / experiment harness notes:
- Run harness: python infra/benchmarks/stochastic_fission_run.py --model 7B --tp 2 --pp 2 --nodes 1 --clients 16 --k-dist "uniform:1-3" --offset-dist "exp:80us" --log-dir /tmp/fission/run_x
- NCCL debug: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO && capture collector to /tmp/nccl.log; post-process: scripts/align_nccl_with_router.py /tmp/nccl.log /tmp/router.log 
- NVLink counters: nvidia-smi dmon + read per-GPU link metrics via nvml at 50ms freq.

Notes to self (quick):
- File raw traces under s3://redwood-infra/experiments/stochastic-fission/ – full tarballs for run ids 20240923-1..5.
- Cross-check PR#3387 that implements router-side micro-batcher – edge case where large requests (>32k tokens) should bypass fission.

Conclusions:
- Stochastic batch fission (K=2, occasional K=3 with exp offsets) is a promising mitigation for repeatable NCCL and NVLink-aligned tail spikes. The throughput cost (~5-10%) is reasonable for high-SLO customers where 99.9p matters.
- Next steps: prototype adaptive-K and KV-aware micro-batching, run a 2-week canary on Dedicated clusters, and add observability surfaces to console for per-route fission metrics.

Questions for the group:
- Thoughts on safety constraints for function-calling routes? (Priya)
- Any objections to defaulting to K=1 for low-tier customers to avoid throughput loss? (SLA implications)
- Interested in a follow-up where we try per-layer randomized schedule offsets (instead of micro-batch level)? Could be more invasive but might reduce collectives even further.

-- Maya
